name: Ivan Nakamura

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for your time, Ivan. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to companies, unions, parties or government. Everything is confidential. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on a live-line crew on the coast, which means we work on lines while they're still switched on, using insulated poles and gloves, so the customers never lose power. Most days it's replacing insulators or moving lines for a new road. In storm season it's all hands, and I've done thirty hours straight after a cyclone came through.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it's the top end of the trade, you have to be calm and exact. I use AI on my phone every day, mostly to study for tickets and to price up jobs for a little side business I'm building. What wears me out is the paperwork and the safety meetings that go on for an hour to say what could be said in five minutes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read it out. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI is a good tool and people expected too much. It still helps you work faster if you use it right. I'd post something like that and move on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it's fine for me. I'd keep building my business on the side, and the live-line work pays well. Nothing to fear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my crew job and grow the side business, hiring one more guy by next winter. I'd keep renting out half my duplex. And I'd sit my substation ticket, because more tickets means more options.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Looking forward, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about the side business.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tree clearing near private power lines, on farms and resorts along the coast. Right now my tree-clearing business is weekends, me and my mate Corey with a chipper and a bucket truck we bought second-hand. I use AI to write quotes and plan routes, which saves me hours every week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything you worry about, AI aside?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly my mum. She's on her own since Dad died, and I want to make sure she never has to worry about money. That's partly why I'm building the business, so the family has something solid.

I'd post that it still **helps you work faster** if you use it well.
think: It's **fine for me**, since live-line work pays well.
I'd keep building **my side business** with nothing to fear.
do: Keep the crew job and **hire one more** for the side business by next winter.
Keep **renting out half** of my duplex.
Sit my **substation ticket** for more options.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a great time to own a business, because the tools cut your costs. Anyone with a trade and some drive can do well. I'd say that loudly, and I'd mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I win. My trade is hands-on and my business gets cheaper to run. The only risk is the big contractors using AI to undercut small guys like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go all in on AI for quoting, scheduling and invoicing in the business. I'd look at a tree-trimming drone. And I'd keep my crew job a couple more years while the business grows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, honestly a bit excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does this change your plans for the business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, it speeds things up. If AI does my office work, I can run two crews on weekends instead of one. Maybe I'd go full time within three years instead of five.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The office people at the company, and maybe the older guys who won't learn anything new. I'd tell them, learn the tools. I'm not going to wait for the government to fix things, and neither should they.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a huge shift, but people who move first will be fine. Adapt or get left behind. That's what I'd say, and I'd mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be uneasy. 2028 is fine for me, AI runs my office. But 2031, robots that climb and cut, means my crew job goes and my business has to compete with whoever owns the best robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now, I'd leave the crew job and go full time with the business within a year. I'd save hard and sell the duplex if I had to, to buy a robot as soon as they're on the market. I'd want to own the machines, not be replaced by them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more fired up than scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the tree business once the robots arrive?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I buy robots early, it gets bigger. If the big contractors buy them first, I'm in trouble. It's a race, and two years isn't much of a head start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about your mum?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd make sure the duplex rent goes to her if things go bad. Family first. She's sixty and she shouldn't have to start over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to build something, so stop complaining and start. I'd be telling the young guys to start a side business now. That's how I see the world.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, this is close to perfect for me. Robots around 2034, I'd be 35, with a proper business and money saved to buy them. I'd be one of the people running robots, not one of the ones they replace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the crew job two more years, then go full time. I'd keep the duplex. And I'd buy the robots the year they come out, with savings, not debt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. This is a good one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do the extra three years give you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time to grow without betting the house. In the fast picture I'd have to sell the duplex. Here I keep it and grow the business from profit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd do differently from the fast picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hire some of the older guys from my crew when they retire, because they know every line on this coast. Robots will need people who know where to send them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long runway, and anyone who doesn't prepare only has themselves to blame. Maybe that sounds harsh, but it's how I see it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be calm. Robots around 2039, I'd be 40, with a solid business and property. I'd have every chance to get ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Grow the business steadily, buy another rental, keep the crew job until about 30. I'd use AI for everything in the office and study robotics in my spare time. I'd plan to be the guy with a fleet of robots by 2040.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, does your plan change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much. It just gets slower and safer. I'd grow from profit and add property.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your own kids one day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn a trade, learn the machines, and own something. Working for someone else is fine, but owning the business is what keeps you safe.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it's a race I might lose to the big contractors. What would help is fair access to buy robots for small firms, not just giant companies getting first dibs, and less red tape for small businesses.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Whether the robots will be any good in a cyclone. I've worked thirty hours straight in a storm, and I'd love to see a robot do that. If they can't, people like me stay useful for a long time.

headlineQuote: I've worked thirty hours straight in a storm, and I'd love to see a robot do that.
portrait: Ivan is a 27-year-old **live-line worker** on the coast who works on energised lines.
He runs a **tree-clearing side business** and rents out half his duplex.
He **uses AI daily** to quote, plan and study, and wants to own robots.
He feels calm in most pictures, **uneasy** only in the fast one where he races big contractors.
His plan centres on **ownership and family**, especially security for his widowed mum.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, a race to buy robots he might lose to big contractors.
whatWouldHelp: **Fair access** for small firms to buy robots.
